'''verification''' (ver″i-fi-kā′shon), ''n.'' [< OF. ''verification'', F. ''vérification'' = Sp. ''verificacion'' = Pg. ''verificação'' = It. ''verificazione'', < ML. *''verificatio''(''n''-), < ''verificare'', make true, verify: see ''verify''.] '''1.''' The act of verifying, or proving to be true; the act of confirming or establishing the authenticity of any powers granted, or of any transaction, by legal or competent evidence; the state of being verified; authentication; confirmation.
{{smaller block|Exceptional phenomena solicit our belief in vain until such time as we chance to conceive them as of kinds already admitted to exist. What science means by ''verification'' is no more than this. {{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychol., II. 301.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''law'': (''a'') A short affidavit appended to a pleading or petition to the effect that the statements in it are true. (''b'') At common law, the formal statement at the end of a plea, “and this he is ready to verify.”

'''verificative''' (ver′i-fi-kạ̄-tiv), ''a.'' [< ML. ''verificatus'', pp. of ''verificare'', verify, + ''-ive''.] Serving to verify; verifying.

'''verifier''' (ver′i-fī-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''verify'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who or that which verifies, or proves or makes appear to be true.—'''2.''' A device for estimating the richness of gas. {{smaller|It consists of a gas-burner so arranged that the amount of gas consumed by a flame of standard length in a given time can be measured and compared as to volume with a gas of known value. It is used for testing gas independently of the photometric value of the gas, and as a verifier of this.}}

'''verify''' (ver′i-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''verified'', ppr. ''verifying''. [< OF. ''verifier'', F. ''vérifier'' = Sp. Pg. ''verificar'' = It. ''verificare'', < ML. ''verificare'', make true, < L. ''verus'', true, + ''facere'', do: see ''-fy''.] '''1.''' To prove to be true; confirm; establish the proof of.
{{smaller block|This is ''verified'' by a number of examples. {{right|''Bacon.''}}
What this learned gentleman supposes in speculation I have known actually ''verified'' in practice. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 367.}}}} '''2.''' To give the appearance of truth to. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Zopirus . . . fayned himselfe in extreame disgrace of his King: for ''verifying'' of which, he caused his own nose and eares to be cut off. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie.}}
'''3.''' To fulfil, as a promise; confirm the truth of, as a prediction.
{{smaller block|And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be ''verified'', which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father.
{{right|1 Ki. viii. 26.}}}}
'''4.''' To confirm the truthfulness of; prove to have spoken truth.
{{smaller block|<poem>So shalt thou best fulfil, best ''verify''
The prophets old.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iii. 177.}}}}
'''5.''' To confirm or establish the authenticity of, as a title or power, by examination or competent evidence.
{{smaller block|To ''verify'' our title with our lives.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 277.}}}}
'''6.''' To ascertain to be correct, or to correct if found erroneous: as, to ''verify'' a statement, quotation, reference, account, or reckoning of any kind; to ''verify'' the items of a bill, or the total amount.—'''7†.''' To maintain; affirm.
{{smaller block|They have ''verified'' unjust things.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 1. 222.}}}}
'''8†.''' To second or strengthen by aid; back; support the credit of.
{{smaller block|<poem>For I have ever ''verified'' my friends,
Of whom he’s chief.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 2. 17.}}}}
'''9.''' In ''law'': (''a'') To make an affidavit regarding (a pleading or petition), and appended to it,<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
